name: Learn five foundational sauces
blurb: Béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise and tomato. Learn these five and you have the parent of hundreds of derivative sauces, plus the three thickening techniques that underpin them.
gear: A heavy saucepan and a whisk
steps: Learn the roux: equal butter and flour, cooked to white, blond or brown depending on the sauce.
Make a béchamel — roux plus milk — whisked smooth, and learn the derivatives: mornay with cheese, soubise with onion.
Make a velouté with a blond roux and light stock, which teaches you why stock quality matters.
Make an espagnole with a brown roux and dark stock, the base of demi-glace.
Make a hollandaise, an emulsion rather than a roux sauce, and learn to hold it without splitting.
Make a proper tomato sauce, reduced slowly, and taste how the acidity and sweetness shift over an hour.
tips: Lumps come from adding cold liquid to hot roux too fast, or not whisking. Add gradually.
A raw-flour taste means the roux was undercooked. Give it a couple of minutes before adding liquid.
Strain if in doubt; it fixes most textural sins.
proof: You make all five without recipes, and produce two derivative sauces from memory.
